## SASE in the Age of AI: Why Architecture Matters More Than Ever


While I hung up my Gartner Analyst hat a handful of years ago, I still feel a strong connection with the work Neil MacDonald and I did to define what has become one of the biggest developments in networking and security in over a quarter of a century: secure access service edge (SASE). With all the hype that AI changes everything, it seems important to examine SASE’s role and requirements in this rapidly changing world. The short answer is:


**In the age of AI, SASE’s fundamental architectural principals remain sound, and architecture matters more than ever!**


Are we now in the age of SASE 2.0? To me, it looks more like SASE 1.2, a step beyond the initial enhancements to the core capabilities (things like advanced analytics and automation) rather than rethinking SASE 1.0’s base architecture.


So, what has changed? AI places increased demands upon security and networking. End users are now a mixture of humans and agents, with agents generating enormous amounts of new, globally distributed traffic. As organizations offload more critical business functions (such as customer support and product fulfillment) to agents, outages will have material consequences on the business. When AI is deployed in industries such as financial services for applications such as high frequency trading, an outage, or even a slowdown, can result in millions of dollars in lost opportunities. The


service delivery requirements (whether for legacy web, cloud or SaaS or modern AI) remain the same. Services must be inline, globally available, consistent, and highly available, with great performance.


We will see a tidal wave of new apps, much like what we saw with SaaS twenty years ago, only increased in number by several orders of magnitude. These agent-driven apps will be created and adopted by lines of business, or individual employees, many of them outside purview of IT. Just as we saw SaaS adoption drive adoption of cloud access security broker (CASB), similar capabilities will be required for this new phase. While users are still important, the shift is now to agents operating either under direction of human users or in an entirely autonomous fashion. Risks associated with AI and agentic workflows are even called out in the recent


[Anthropic S1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026067168/anthropicpbc-sx1.htm) filing.


*“These risks may be heightened where multiple AI agents operate together. Agents that interact or coordinate with one another may amplify, propagate, or reinforce misaligned behavior across the group, pursue objectives collectively in ways not intended or endorsed by any user, or take coordinated actions against systems or targets unrelated to their assigned tasks, in each case, in ways that may be difficult to anticipate, detect, or contain. Incidents of this kind have occurred, and we expect the deployment and interaction of larger numbers of autonomous agents to increase these risks over time.”*


If predictions are correct, users may each employ 100 agents, so the scale and scope of the risk is immense. AI swarm-based applications could activate thousands of agents, each with hundreds of interactions. Negative outcomes could include data leaks, theft of proprietary models, compliance violations, abuse/misuse, cost overruns, and malicious code/threats.


The good news is that while new services will be required for AI, SASE’s fundamental architecture is optimized for just such an environment. SASE’s key tenets remain:


- **SASE is a highly distributed, primarily cloud delivered service.** This enables global reach, scalability of services and fault tolerance/high availability. Neil and I realized the mantra for SASE was “Cloud delivered whenever you can; on premises only when you must” (and at times, you must: some agents will live on the desktop, using MCP, models and other tools, so cloud delivered services won’t see these applications).


- **Access is granted through least privilege, zero trust network access (ZTNA) with continuous inspection and enforcement, based upon context and behavior.** It’s not enough to grant permission to an agent’s initial actions. Access must now be JIT/JEA-based with constant context-based monitoring to ensure the agent’s behavior doesn’t change to prohibited actions. This means parsing and decoding API/JSON, just as is done with the SaaS applications that drove adoption of CASB. For AI it’s not just about understanding the user/agent and the destination, but also understanding the transaction in detail, including understanding of the task (e.g. using inference, downloading or uploading an asset, training an LLM with sensitive data, etc.).


- **Services, including end-to-end traffic routing, are located at the edge of the network, close to the users and agents, and data and services are delivered in a single pass.** First, this is required to ensure data sovereignty. But with the increase of global tensions and national/regional sovereignty requirements, preventing agents from interacting with agents outside the sovereign area will become increasingly critical. Even traversing networks in prohibited areas may represent unacceptable risk.


Additionally, single-pass edge delivery is required to deliver consistent performance. Just as with SaaS applications, AI application performance that results in multiple seconds of blinking cursors will not satisfy human users. A higher threshold of performance-based guarantees will become critical as time-sensitive AI applications take hold, including, but not limited to, the previously mentioned high-frequency trading scenario. Consider two pharmaceutical companies leveraging the same AI tools to pursue a miracle drug. They discover the drug at almost the same time. But one company gets the answer milliseconds sooner and its patent agent is therefore able to file and secure a patent application sooner. The payoff could be tens of billions of dollars for them, and none for their rival!


While the application environment has changed with AI, the core security, systems and networking architectural principles of SASE still hold true. Just as with early SASE deployment, sub-optimal implementations (centralized, or on premises) of SASE 1.2 may initially deliver acceptable results, but as broader AI services are deployed, crippling limitations in security and performance will surface. These will inject great risk and expenses for companies that evaluate SASE 1.2 as a list of features without carefully considering vendors’ underlying architecture. In my experience, doing the hard work up front always pays off over the long term. As your organization dives headfirst into embracing AI and related security and network tools like SASE, pay special attention to the architecture, because architecture matters more than ever!
